column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which observation about a sea star is qualitative?
column14: It has 5 arms.
column15: One of its arms is 9 cm long.
column16: Its skin feels rough and bumpy.
column17: It moved 12 cm in one hour.
column28: Rough and bumpy describes a quality with words, so it is qualitative. The other choices come from counting or measuring, so they are quantitative. A common mistake is calling a count like 5 arms qualitative; any count is a number.
column29: Look for the choice that describes the sea star with words and no numbers.

column9: A student checks a classroom fish tank. Which observation is quantitative?
column14: The water looks a little cloudy.
column15: The fish have bright orange scales.
column16: The gravel on the bottom is smooth.
column17: The water temperature is 24 °C.
column28: 24 °C is a measured number, so it is quantitative. Cloudy, orange, and smooth describe qualities with words, so they are qualitative.
column29: Which observation needed a tool, like a thermometer, and gives a number?

column9: Data that describe a characteristic using words instead of numbers are called ___ data.
column28: Qualitative data describe qualities with words, like color, smell, or texture. A common mistake is mixing it up with quantitative data, which are numbers from counting or measuring.
column29: There are two types of data. This is the type that does NOT use numbers.

column9: On a line graph, which axis usually shows the dependent variable?
column14: The x-axis (horizontal)
column15: The y-axis (vertical)
column16: Neither; it only goes in the title
column17: Both axes
column28: The dependent variable (what is measured) goes on the y-axis, the vertical one. The independent variable goes on the x-axis. Students often switch these two.
column29: The thing you measure goes up and down on the graph.

column9: A student tests how the number of hours of light per day affects how many radish seeds sprout. Which variable goes on the x-axis?
column14: Hours of light per day
column15: Number of seeds that sprouted
column16: Type of soil used
column17: The date the seeds were planted
column28: Hours of light is the independent variable (the one the student changes), so it goes on the x-axis. The number of seeds that sprouted is measured, so it goes on the y-axis. A common mistake is putting the result on the x-axis.
column29: Which variable did the student choose and change on purpose?

column9: An experiment tests whether the amount of salt in water changes how many brine shrimp eggs hatch. Which graph title is best?
column14: Brine Shrimp Lab
column15: The Effect of Brine Shrimp Hatching on Salt Concentration
column16: Salt Water Results
column17: The Effect of Salt Concentration on Brine Shrimp Hatching
column28: A good title names the independent variable (salt concentration) and the dependent variable (brine shrimp hatching): "The Effect of [IV] on [DV]." The second choice flips the two variables, which is a common mistake. The other titles do not tell what was tested.
column29: A strong title tells which variable was changed and which was measured, in that order.

column9: A school nurse wants to show what percent of students have each blood type (A, B, AB, and O). Which graph shows these parts of a whole best?
column14: Line graph
column15: Pie chart
column16: Bar graph with one bar for each day of school
column17: A single number for the whole school
column28: A pie chart shows how a whole (all the students) is split into parts, and its slices add up to 100%. A line graph is for change over time, and the other choices don't show the blood types at all.
column29: The percents for all four blood types together make up the whole school.

column9: A student measures the average height of sunflowers grown in four different brands of potting soil. Which graph best compares the four brands?
column14: Pie chart
column15: Line graph connecting the four brands
column16: Bar graph with one bar for each brand
column17: No graph; just list the brand names
column28: The brands are separate categories, so a bar graph with one bar per brand compares them best. A line graph would connect brands as if there were values in between them, which is a common mistake. A pie chart is for parts of a whole.
column29: Are the soil brands separate groups, or a number that changes smoothly?

column9: Which graph would best show how a hibernating bear's body temperature changed each week during the winter?
column14: Pie chart
column15: Bar graph with one bar for each bear species
column16: Line graph with weeks on the x-axis
column17: Line graph with body temperature on the x-axis
column28: Change over time is shown best with a line graph, and time (weeks) is the independent variable, so it goes on the x-axis. The last choice puts the measured variable on the wrong axis, a common mistake.
column29: Something is changing over time. Which graph and which axis fit time?

column9: What is the main reason scientists record results in a data table?
column14: To organize measurements so they are easy to read and compare
column15: To make the experiment take longer
column16: To replace the need for a hypothesis
column17: To hide results that do not match the prediction
column28: A data table organizes measurements in rows and columns so they are easy to read and compare. It never replaces a hypothesis, and hiding results is dishonest.
column29: Think about what rows and columns do for a pile of numbers.

column9: To find the ___ of a set of trials, add all the values and then divide by the number of values.
column28: The mean (average) is the sum of the values divided by how many values there are. A common mistake is confusing it with the range, which is the highest value minus the lowest.
column29: This one number stands for the typical result of all your trials.

column9: A student measured a resting heart rate four times: 70, 74, 78, and 82 beats per minute. What is the mean heart rate, in beats per minute?
column28: 70 + 74 + 78 + 82 = 304, and 304 ÷ 4 = 76 beats per minute. A common mistake is dividing by 3 instead of 4, the number of values.
column29: Add all four values, then divide by how many values you added.

column9: A lab group timed one snail crawling across a 30 cm board, got 4 minutes, and wrote that snails take 4 minutes to cross. What is the best reason they should run more trials before reporting that?
column14: Because the first trial is always wrong
column15: So one mistake or unusual result does not decide the conclusion
column16: So they can pick the trial that matches their hypothesis
column17: So the data table looks longer
column28: Repeated trials make results more reliable, so one mistake or odd result can't decide the conclusion. Picking only the trial that matches the hypothesis is a common but dishonest mistake.
column29: What could go wrong if you only ran the experiment once?

column9: Which column heading is best for a data table that records the mass of mice?
column14: Mass
column15: Mouse stuff
column16: How heavy
column17: Mass of mouse (g)
column28: A good heading names what was measured and gives its unit in parentheses, like "Mass of mouse (g)." Plain "Mass" is a common mistake because the reader can't tell if it is grams or kilograms.
column29: Which heading tells the reader both what was measured and the unit?

column9: A student graphs the hours of daylight per day (x-axis) against the number of flowers on a petunia plant (y-axis). The line rises from left to right. What does this show?
column14: As daylight increased, the number of flowers decreased.
column15: Daylight had no effect on the number of flowers.
column16: As daylight increased, the number of flowers increased.
column17: The flowers caused the days to get longer.
column28: A line that rises from left to right means the dependent variable (flowers) goes up as the independent variable (daylight) goes up. A common mistake is reading a rising line as a decrease.
column29: Follow the line from left to right. Is it going up or down?

column9: On a line graph of a person's pulse at different room light levels, the line is flat (horizontal). What does this show?
column14: Pulse went up as the light increased.
column15: Pulse stayed about the same as the light changed.
column16: Pulse went down as the light increased.
column17: The graph has no data on it.
column28: A flat line means the dependent variable (pulse) did not change as the independent variable (light) changed. A common mistake is thinking a flat line means there are no data; the points are there, they just stay level.
column29: If the line never goes up or down, what is happening to the pulse?

column9: A pie chart is the best graph for showing how a kitten's mass changes from week to week.
column28: False. Change over time is best shown with a line graph, with time on the x-axis. A pie chart shows how one whole is split into parts.
column29: Is the mass changing over time, or is it a part of a whole?

column9: Which set of numbers is an evenly spaced scale for a graph's y-axis?
column28: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 goes up by the same amount (10) every step and is in order. The other scales jump by different amounts or are out of order, which would bend the shape of the graph.
column29: Check the jump from each number to the next. Is it always the same?

column9: Each axis label on a graph should name the variable and include its ___, such as cm, g, or °C.
column28: Axis labels need units (like cm, g, or °C) so the reader knows exactly how the variable was measured. Leaving them off is one of the most common graphing mistakes.
column29: What do cm, g, and °C have in common?

column9: Which sentence is written the way a scientist should state a conclusion?
column14: The data support the hypothesis that plants grow taller with more light.
column15: This experiment proves that light makes plants grow.
column16: I feel like the plants liked the light.
column17: Everyone already knows plants need light.
column28: Scientists say the data support (or do not support) a hypothesis. One experiment can't "prove" something forever, so "proves" is a common mistake. Feelings and "everyone knows" are not evidence.
column29: Look for the sentence that is based on the data, not on feelings or certainty.

column9: Which sentence communicates the result of a watering experiment most clearly and concisely?
column14: The plants grew a lot.
column15: We did the experiment, and then we watered the plants each day, and then we measured them, and some were taller and some were not.
column16: I think watering plants is good for them.
column17: Plants given 10 mL of water per day grew an average of 6 cm in two weeks, twice as much as plants given 2 mL per day.
column28: The best sentence is short but gives the groups, the measured result, and the numbers with units. "Grew a lot" is too vague, the long sentence never states a result, and "I think" is an opinion.
column29: Pick the one sentence that tells WHAT happened using numbers and units.

column9: Match each data word to its meaning.
column14: Trend :: The overall pattern or direction in a set of data
column15: Outlier :: A value that is very different from the rest of the data
column16: Trial :: One run of the experiment
column17: Raw data :: The measurements recorded before any math is done
column28: A trend is the overall pattern; an outlier is a value far from the others; a trial is one run of the experiment; raw data are the original measurements before averaging. Students often mix up trend and outlier.
column29: An outlier "lies outside" the rest of the data.

column9: A student observes a leopard frog. Select every qualitative observation. Select all that apply.
column14: Its skin is slimy.
column15: It is green with dark spots.
column16: It jumped 45 cm.
column17: It has 4 legs.
column18: Its croak is low and deep.
column19: It has a mass of 30 g.
column28: Slimy, green with dark spots, and a low, deep croak describe qualities with words, so they are qualitative. 45 cm, 4 legs, and 30 g are numbers from measuring or counting, so they are quantitative. Counting legs is a common trap.
column29: Cross out anything that has a number in it.

column9: A student wants quantitative data about how ripe bananas are. Which method gives quantitative data?
column14: Describe the color of each banana.
column15: Smell each banana and write down the smell.
column16: Count the brown spots on each banana.
column17: Ask a friend if the bananas look ripe.
column28: Counting brown spots gives a number, so it is quantitative. Color, smell, and a friend's opinion are described with words, so they are qualitative.
column29: Which method ends with a number?

column9: An Elodea plant was placed at different distances from a lamp. Bubbles given off per minute: 10 cm: 40, 20 cm: 28, 30 cm: 15, 40 cm: 6. At what distance did the plant give off 15 bubbles per minute?
column14: 10 cm
column15: 20 cm
column16: 30 cm
column17: 40 cm
column28: Find 15 in the bubbles column and read across: it matches 30 cm. A common mistake is reading the wrong row or mixing up which number is the distance and which is the bubble count.
column29: Find the number 15 first, then look at the distance that goes with it.

column9: A pond's dissolved oxygen was measured four times: March 9 mg/L, May 7 mg/L, July 5 mg/L, August 4 mg/L. Which describes the trend?
column14: It went up and then down.
column15: It increased over time.
column16: It decreased over time.
column17: It stayed the same.
column28: Each measurement is lower than the one before (9, 7, 5, 4), so dissolved oxygen decreased over time. A common mistake is focusing on one pair of numbers instead of the whole pattern.
column29: Read the numbers in order from March to August.

column9: The range of a data set is the highest value minus the lowest value. A student counted ladybugs on five rose bushes: 3, 8, 5, 12, and 6. What is the range?
column28: Highest (12) − lowest (3) = 9. A common mistake is subtracting the first and last numbers in the list (6 − 3) instead of the highest and lowest.
column29: Find the biggest and smallest numbers first, wherever they are in the list.

column9: Which part of a lab report presents the data in organized tables and graphs?
column14: Hypothesis
column15: Materials
column16: Results
column17: Question
column28: The Results section shows the data in tables and graphs. The hypothesis is the prediction, the materials list the equipment, and the question is what the experiment asks.
column29: Which section shows what actually happened?

column9: Why do scientists share their methods and results with other scientists?
column14: So others can check the work and repeat the experiment
column15: So no one else will ever test the same idea
column16: So they don't have to write a conclusion
column17: Because results are only true if many people like them
column28: Sharing methods and results lets other scientists check the work and repeat the experiment to see if they get the same results. Science does not depend on whether people like a result.
column29: If another scientist wanted to test your results, what would they need?

column9: In a student's data, the average hours of sleep per day were: hamster 14, gerbil 12, mouse 13, rat 11. Which sentence correctly describes the data?
column14: Rats slept the most.
column15: All four rodents slept the same amount.
column16: Gerbils slept 2 hours more than hamsters.
column17: Hamsters slept the most, 3 hours more than rats.
column28: Hamsters had the largest value (14 hours), and 14 − 11 = 3 hours more than rats. A common mistake is comparing in the wrong direction, like saying gerbils slept more than hamsters.
column29: Find the biggest number first, then check the difference.

column9: The largest value a student needs to graph is 87 mm. Which y-axis scale fits the data best?
column14: 0 to 20, counting by 2s
column15: 0 to 100, counting by 10s
column16: 0 to 1,000, counting by 100s
column17: 50 to 60, counting by 1s
column28: 0 to 100 by 10s fits 87 mm and uses most of the graph. 0 to 20 and 50 to 60 are too small to fit 87, and 0 to 1,000 would squash all the data near the bottom.
column29: The scale has to reach past 87 without leaving most of the graph empty.

column9: Which set of chicken egg masses contains an outlier?
column28: 19 g is far from the other values (55 to 58 g), so it is an outlier. In the other sets, all the values are close together. A common mistake is calling the biggest number in a normal set an outlier.
column29: Look for one number that doesn't fit with the others in its set.

column9: A graph is titled "The Effect of Caffeine on Daphnia Heart Rate." What is the independent variable?
column14: Amount of caffeine
column15: Daphnia heart rate
column16: The type of microscope
column17: The temperature of the water
column28: In "The Effect of A on B," A is the independent variable (what was changed) and B is the dependent variable (what was measured). Here, caffeine was changed. A common mistake is picking heart rate, which is measured.
column29: Which variable comes right after "The Effect of"?

column9: In the graph title "The Effect of Sleep on Reaction Time," the dependent variable is ___.
column28: Reaction time is what was measured, so it is the dependent variable. Sleep was changed, so it is the independent variable. A common mistake is choosing the first variable named in the title.
column29: In "The Effect of A on B," which one is being measured?

column9: Before a study is published, other scientists in the same field check its methods and results. What is this process called?
column14: Peer review
column15: Hypothesis
column16: Control group
column17: Inference
column28: Peer review is when other experts check a study before it is published. A hypothesis is a testable prediction, and a control group is a comparison group in the experiment.
column29: A "peer" is someone at the same level as you.

column9: Match each measurement to the metric unit you would record it in.
column14: Length of a leaf :: centimeters (cm)
column15: Volume of water in a beaker :: milliliters (mL)
column16: Temperature of pond water :: degrees Celsius (°C)
column17: Time for a reaction to finish :: seconds (s)
column28: Length uses cm, liquid volume uses mL, temperature uses °C, and time uses seconds. A common mix-up is using mL for length or cm for volume.
column29: Think about which tool you'd use for each: ruler, graduated cylinder, thermometer, or stopwatch.

column9: On a line graph of a calf's mass, one point sits above 6 weeks on the x-axis and across from 80 kg on the y-axis. What does this point mean?
column14: The calf gained 6 kg in 80 weeks.
column15: At 6 weeks old, the calf had a mass of 80 kg.
column16: The calf gained 80 kg every week.
column17: The calf lost 80 kg in 6 weeks.
column28: Each point pairs an x-value with a y-value: at 6 weeks (x), the mass was 80 kg (y). One point shows a single measurement, not a gain or loss, which is a common misreading.
column29: Read the x-value and the y-value for that one point together.

column9: Put these parts of a lab report in the order they usually appear.
column14: Conclusion
column15: Hypothesis
column16: Results
column17: Question
column28: A lab report starts with the Question, then the Hypothesis (the prediction), then the Procedure (the steps), then the Results (the data), and ends with the Conclusion. A common mistake is putting Results before Procedure.
column29: You need a question before you can predict, and you need data before you can conclude.

column9: Match each part of a graph to its job.
column14: Title :: Tells what the graph is about
column15: Axis label :: Tells which variable is shown along that edge of the graph
column16: Key (legend) :: Tells what each line, color, or symbol stands for
column17: Data point :: Shows one measurement on the graph
column28: The title tells what the graph is about, axis labels name the variables, the key explains lines or colors, and each data point is one measurement. Students often confuse the title with the axis labels.
column29: Which part would you need if a graph had two lines in different colors?

column9: A pie chart shows the fish caught in a lake survey: bluegill 50%, perch 25%, bass 15%, and walleye. What percent should the walleye slice be?
column28: All the slices of a pie chart make one whole, 100%. 50 + 25 + 15 = 90, so walleye = 100 − 90 = 10%. A common mistake is forgetting that the whole must be exactly 100%.
column29: What must all the slices of a pie add up to?

column9: A student writes, "The hand warmer got really hot." Which rewrite communicates the data more precisely?
column14: The hand warmer got super, super hot.
column15: The hand warmer was hotter than I expected.
column16: The hand warmer warmed from 21 °C to 48 °C in 5 minutes.
column17: The hand warmer changed temperature.
column28: Giving the starting and ending temperatures with units and the time makes the result precise and still short. Adding words like "super" or "than I expected" doesn't add data.
column29: Which rewrite would let a reader know exactly how hot, and how fast?

column9: What is the main advantage of showing data in a graph instead of only a list of numbers?
column14: Patterns and trends are easier to see.
column15: A graph does not need any labels.
column16: A graph makes the data more accurate.
column17: A graph removes the need for units.
column28: Graphs make patterns and trends easy to see at a glance. A graph does not make data more accurate, and it still needs labels and units.
column29: What can your eyes pick out faster on a picture than in a list?

column9: A student counts the dandelions in five 1-meter squares on the football field. What kind of data is this?
column14: Qualitative, because dandelions are plants
column15: Quantitative, because the data are counts (numbers)
column16: Qualitative, because the student used only their eyes
column17: Neither; counts are not data
column28: Counts are numbers, so they are quantitative data. A common mistake is thinking data are qualitative because no tool was used; counting by eye still gives a number.
column29: Will the student's results be words or numbers?

column9: In a student's data table, the average resting heart rate is 600 beats per minute for a mouse, 150 for a cat, and 40 for a horse. Which sentence correctly communicates the data?
column14: A horse's heart beats faster than a cat's.
column15: All three animals have about the same heart rate.
column16: A cat's resting heart rate (150 beats per minute) is slower than a mouse's (600 beats per minute).
column17: A mouse's resting heart rate is 150 beats per minute.
column28: 150 is less than 600, so the cat's heart rate is slower than the mouse's, and the sentence gives the numbers with units. The other choices misread the table or attach a number to the wrong animal.
column29: Check each sentence against the numbers in the table.

column9: The mean of 4, 4, and 10 is 6.
column28: True. 4 + 4 + 10 = 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6. A common mistake is answering 4, the value that shows up most often; that is not the mean.
column29: Find the total first, then share it equally among the 3 values.

column9: A student counted how many of 50 bean seeds sprouted at each temperature: 5 °C: 4, 15 °C: 22, 25 °C: 46, 35 °C: 30, 45 °C: 3. Which statement describes the pattern?
column14: Sprouting increased steadily as temperature increased.
column15: Sprouting increased up to 25 °C, then decreased at higher temperatures.
column16: Sprouting decreased as temperature increased.
column17: Temperature had no effect on sprouting.
column28: Sprouting went up from 4 to 46 seeds between 5 °C and 25 °C, then dropped to 30 and 3. A common mistake is describing only the first half of the data and saying it "increased steadily."
column29: Read the whole row. Does the number keep going up all the way to 45 °C?

column9: Hypothesis: If fruit flies are kept warmer, then they will produce more offspring. Results: 18 °C: 40 offspring, 24 °C: 95 offspring, 30 °C: 30 offspring. Which conclusion is best?
column14: The hypothesis was only partly supported: offspring rose from 18 °C to 24 °C but dropped sharply at 30 °C.
column15: The hypothesis was fully supported because warmer flies always had more offspring.
column16: The hypothesis was not supported because 18 °C had the most offspring.
column17: No conclusion can be made because the numbers are different.
column28: Offspring increased from 18 °C to 24 °C (supports the hypothesis) but fell at 30 °C (does not), so the hypothesis is only partly supported. A common mistake is ignoring the 30 °C result. 18 °C did not have the most offspring.
column29: Does the hypothesis hold for every temperature step, or only some?

column9: Four earthworms were measured: 9.5 cm, 11.0 cm, 10.5 cm, and 9.0 cm. What is their mean length, in cm?
column28: 9.5 + 11.0 + 10.5 + 9.0 = 40.0 cm, and 40.0 ÷ 4 = 10.0 cm. A common mistake is a decimal slip when adding, so line up the decimal points.
column29: Add the four lengths carefully, then divide by 4.

column9: Out of 40 seeds planted, 30 sprouted. What percent of the seeds sprouted?
column28: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, and 0.75 × 100 = 75%. A common mistake is dividing the wrong way (40 ÷ 30), which gives a number over 100%.
column29: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.

column9: A radish seedling was 0 cm tall on day 0, 4 cm on day 4, and 8 cm on day 8, growing at a steady rate. About how tall was it on day 6?
column14: 4 cm
column15: 5 cm
column16: 6 cm
column17: 8 cm
column28: The seedling grew 1 cm per day (4 cm every 4 days), so on day 6 it was about 6 cm. Day 6 is between day 4 (4 cm) and day 8 (8 cm), so the answer must be between those values. Choosing 4 or 8 is a common mistake.
column29: How many cm did it grow each day?

column9: A bacteria colony was counted every hour: 100, 200, 400, 800 cells. If the pattern continues, how many cells will there be at the next count?
column28: The count doubles each hour (100 → 200 → 400 → 800), so the next count is 800 × 2 = 1,600. A common mistake is adding the same amount each time instead of doubling.
column29: Compare each number to the one before it. Is it adding or multiplying?

column9: Select every data set that is best shown with a line graph. Select all that apply.
column14: A trout's length measured each month for a year
column15: The number of trees of each species in a park
column16: A runner's heart rate measured every minute during a race
column17: The percent of a lake's fish that belong to each species
column18: Plant height after adding 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 mL of fertilizer
column19: The favorite fruit of each student in a class
column28: Line graphs fit data where the x-variable is a number that changes smoothly, like time or mL of fertilizer. Tree species and favorite fruits are separate categories (bar graph), and percent of each fish species is parts of a whole (pie chart). A common miss is the fertilizer set, which is numbers, not categories.
column29: Ask: is the x-variable a number with in-between values, or a list of separate groups?

column9: On a graph of a seedling's growth, the x-axis is marked 0, 1, 2, 5, and 10 days, with the marks evenly spaced apart. What is wrong?
column14: Nothing; the marks are evenly spaced.
column15: The spaces stand for different amounts of time, so the shape of the graph is distorted.
column16: The x-axis should show plant height instead.
column17: The experiment should have lasted more than 10 days.
column28: The marks are evenly spaced but the numbers jump by 1, 1, 3, and 5 days, so each space means a different amount of time. That bends the shape of the line and can mislead the reader. Equal spaces must stand for equal amounts.
column29: Does each space on the axis stand for the same number of days?

column9: A student will test how 0, 2, 4, and 6 minutes of jumping jacks affect breathing rate, with 3 trials for each time. Which set of column headings is best for the data table?
column14: Breathing rate | Jumping jacks | Notes
column15: Trial | Good or bad | Average
column16: Exercise time (min) | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Average breathing rate (breaths/min)
column17: Average breathing rate (breaths/min) | Student's opinion
column28: The best table puts the independent variable (exercise time, with units) first, has a column for each trial, and ends with the average of the dependent variable, with units. The other choices are missing trials, units, or the independent variable.
column29: The table needs the variable that was changed, room for every trial, and an average, all with units.

column9: Hypothesis: If pill bugs prefer dark places, then more of them will gather on the dark side of a tray. Results: in 3 trials, an average of 9 out of 10 pill bugs moved to the dark side within 10 minutes. Which conclusion is best?
column14: Pill bugs are cool and like the dark.
column15: The hypothesis was proven true for all animals.
column16: The pill bugs moved around the tray.
column17: The hypothesis was supported: on average, 9 of 10 pill bugs moved to the dark side within 10 minutes.
column28: A good conclusion states whether the hypothesis was supported and backs it up with the data. The others are opinions, too broad ("all animals," "proven"), or leave out the result.
column29: A strong conclusion has a claim AND a number to back it up.

column9: A sunflower grew from 12 cm to 30 cm over 6 days. What was its average growth, in cm per day?
column28: It grew 30 − 12 = 18 cm in 6 days, and 18 ÷ 6 = 3 cm per day. A common mistake is dividing the final height (30 ÷ 6 = 5) instead of the amount it grew.
column29: First find how much it grew, then divide by the number of days.

column9: Paper disks soaked in different liquids were placed on a dish of bacteria. A clear ring around a disk means bacteria could not grow there. Ring widths: water 0 mm, garlic extract 12 mm, mouthwash 18 mm, soap 6 mm. Which sentence communicates the results correctly and concisely?
column14: Mouthwash stopped bacteria growth the most (18 mm ring), and water did not stop growth at all (0 mm).
column15: Soap worked best because it is used for cleaning.
column16: Garlic extract had the widest ring, so it stopped the most bacteria.
column17: All the liquids stopped bacteria the same amount.
column28: Mouthwash had the widest clear ring (18 mm) and water had none (0 mm), and the sentence gives those numbers. Soap had only 6 mm, and garlic (12 mm) was not the widest. Saying soap worked best is a guess, not data.
column29: Find the widest and the narrowest rings in the data.

column9: Which sentence belongs in the Results section of a lab report rather than the Conclusion?
column14: This suggests that seeds absorb water before they sprout.
column15: Our hypothesis was supported.
column16: The average mass of the seeds soaked in water was 2.4 g.
column17: Next time, we would use more seeds.
column28: Results report the data ("the average mass was 2.4 g"). Saying what the data suggest, whether the hypothesis was supported, and how to improve the experiment all belong in the Conclusion.
column29: Results tell WHAT was measured. Conclusions tell what it MEANS.

column9: Put these parts of a lab conclusion in a logical order.
column14: Explain why the evidence supports or does not support the claim (reasoning)
column15: Give specific data as evidence
column16: State whether the hypothesis was supported (claim)
column17: Describe possible errors and how to improve the experiment
column28: A clear conclusion starts with the claim (was the hypothesis supported?), then gives evidence (the data), then the reasoning that connects them, and ends with errors and improvements. A common mistake is giving the data before saying what they show.
column29: Claim first, then evidence, then reasoning. Where do errors fit best?

column9: A graph has "Amount of Salt in Water (g/L)" on the x-axis and "Number of Seeds That Sprouted" on the y-axis. What question was the experiment most likely testing?
column14: How does the amount of salt in water affect how many seeds sprout?
column15: How does the number of seeds that sprout affect the amount of salt in water?
column16: Do seeds grow taller in sunlight?
column17: How much salt is in seawater?
column28: The x-axis shows the independent variable (salt) and the y-axis shows the dependent variable (seeds sprouted), so the question is how salt affects sprouting. The second choice reverses cause and effect, a common mistake.
column29: The x-axis is what was changed; the y-axis is what was measured.

column9: A graph's y-axis goes from 0 at the bottom to 50 at the top and is divided into 10 equal spaces. How much does each space stand for?
column28: 50 ÷ 10 spaces = 5 per space. A common mistake is assuming each space is worth 1 or 10 without doing the division.
column29: Divide the total height of the scale by the number of spaces.

column9: A student's conclusion is three pages long and lists every single measurement from every trial. What is the best advice for making it concise?
column14: Add even more detail so nothing is missed.
column15: Summarize the key results, like averages and the overall trend, in a few sentences, and leave the raw numbers in the data table.
column16: Remove all numbers and only describe how the lab felt.
column17: Replace the conclusion with the hypothesis.
column28: A concise conclusion gives the key results (averages, trend) and whether the hypothesis was supported; the raw data stay in the table. Removing all numbers is a common over-correction because it leaves no evidence.
column29: Where do all the individual measurements already appear?

column9: A student tested how the amount of sugar affects how much gas yeast makes, measured by how wide a balloon on the flask gets. Select every sentence that belongs in a concise conclusion. Select all that apply.
column14: As sugar increased from 0 g to 10 g, the balloon's width increased from 0 cm to 18 cm.
column15: The hypothesis that more sugar would produce more gas was supported.
column16: My lab partner was late, so we started at 10:15.
column17: A balloon may have leaked in trial 2, which could explain its smaller size.
column19: This was the most fun lab ever.
column28: A concise conclusion includes the result with data, whether the hypothesis was supported, and possible sources of error. When the lab started, smells, and opinions about fun don't help explain the results.
column29: Keep only the sentences that are about the results or how trustworthy they are.

column9: Hypothesis: If plants are grown under blue light, then they will grow taller than plants under red or white light. Average heights: red light 14 cm, white light 12 cm, blue light 9 cm. Which statement correctly communicates the result?
column14: The hypothesis was supported because blue light was used.
column15: The hypothesis was supported because all the plants grew.
column16: Plants under white light grew the tallest.
column17: The hypothesis was not supported; plants under red light grew tallest (14 cm) and plants under blue light grew the least (9 cm).
column28: Blue light gave the shortest plants (9 cm), so the hypothesis was not supported. A common mistake is saying a hypothesis is supported just because the experiment was done or the plants grew. White light (12 cm) was not the tallest.
column29: Which light color gave the tallest plants? Was that what the hypothesis predicted?

column9: A student measured how far a snail moved in 5 minutes on three surfaces, with 3 trials each: wet glass 12, 14, 13 cm; dry glass 4, 6, 5 cm; sandpaper 0, 1, 2 cm. Which statement reports the averages correctly?
column14: Wet glass 13 cm, dry glass 5 cm, sandpaper 1 cm
column15: Wet glass 39 cm, dry glass 15 cm, sandpaper 3 cm
column16: Wet glass 14 cm, dry glass 6 cm, sandpaper 2 cm
column17: Wet glass 12 cm, dry glass 4 cm, sandpaper 0 cm
column28: Wet glass: 39 ÷ 3 = 13 cm; dry glass: 15 ÷ 3 = 5 cm; sandpaper: 3 ÷ 3 = 1 cm. A common mistake is reporting the totals (39, 15, 3) and forgetting to divide by the number of trials.
column29: Add each surface's three trials, then divide by 3.

column9: A student made a line graph that connects points for the number of ladybugs found on four kinds of plants: rose, tomato, milkweed, and bean. What is the problem?
column14: Nothing is wrong; line graphs work for any data.
column15: The plant kinds are separate categories, so a line connecting them suggests in-between values that don't exist; a bar graph fits better.
column16: It should be a pie chart because there are four plants.
column17: Ladybugs can't be counted, so no graph will work.
column28: There is nothing "between" a rose and a tomato plant, so connecting the points with a line is misleading. Separate categories are compared best with a bar graph. A pie chart would only fit if the data were parts of a whole.
column29: What would a point halfway between "rose" and "tomato" even mean?

column9: A student's line graph is titled "Graph 1." The x-axis is labeled "Time" and the y-axis is labeled "Growth." Two lines (with and without fertilizer) are drawn in different colors, but there is no key. Select every change that would improve the graph. Select all that apply.
column14: Change the title to name the variables, like "The Effect of Fertilizer on Plant Height Over Time"
column15: Add units to the x-axis label, like "Time (days)"
column16: Add units to the y-axis label, like "Plant Height (cm)"
column17: Add a key that shows which color is which group
column18: Draw both lines in the same color
column19: Remove the y-axis label to make the graph cleaner
column28: The graph needs a descriptive title, units on both axes, and a key so the reader can tell the two lines apart. Making both lines the same color or removing a label would make it harder to read, not easier.
column29: Which changes help a reader understand the graph without asking you any questions?

column9: Two studies tested whether a new sunscreen prevents sunburn. Study A tested 5 people. Study B tested 500 people. Both found fewer sunburns with the sunscreen. Which study's results are more trustworthy to communicate, and why?
column14: Study A, because smaller studies are easier to check
column15: They are equally trustworthy because both found the same thing
column16: Study B, because a larger sample makes it less likely that the results happened by chance
column17: Neither, because sunburn can't be measured
column28: A larger sample size makes results more reliable, because a few unusual people can't swing the outcome. A common mistake is thinking two studies are equal just because they found the same thing.
column29: With only 5 people, how much could one unusual person change the result?

column9: A chick's mass was 40 g on day 0, 150 g on day 7, 380 g on day 14, and 700 g on day 21. Which claim is NOT supported by these data?
column14: The chick gained mass every week.
column15: The chick gained more mass in week 3 than in week 1.
column16: The chick's mass more than doubled from day 7 to day 14.
column17: The chick gained the same amount of mass each week.
column28: The weekly gains were 110 g, 230 g, and 320 g, so they were not the same each week. The other claims check out: mass rose every week, week 3 (320 g) beat week 1 (110 g), and 150 g → 380 g is more than double.
column29: Subtract to find how much mass the chick gained in each week.

column9: Match each research question to the display that would show its data best.
column14: How does a black bear's body mass change from spring to fall? :: Line graph
column15: Which of four lakes has the most walleye? :: Bar graph
column16: What percent of a wolf pack's diet is deer, beaver, and other prey? :: Pie chart
column17: What were the exact measurements from every trial? :: Data table
column28: Change over time → line graph; comparing separate groups (lakes) → bar graph; parts of a whole (percent of a diet) → pie chart; every exact measurement → data table. A common mix-up is using a line graph for separate groups.
column29: Look for clue words: "change over time," "which of four," "percent of," and "exact measurements."

column9: A student's results do not match her hypothesis. What should she do when she writes up the experiment?
column14: Change the data so they match the hypothesis.
column15: Leave the experiment out of her report.
column16: Report the data honestly and state that the hypothesis was not supported.
column17: Rewrite the hypothesis so it matches the data and say it was supported.
column28: Results that don't support a hypothesis are still useful and must be reported honestly. Changing data, hiding the experiment, or rewriting the hypothesis afterward are all dishonest. A common mistake is thinking an unsupported hypothesis means the experiment "failed."
column29: Is a hypothesis that turns out wrong still useful information?

column9: A student made a vertical bar graph (bars that rise up from the x-axis) of the average number of eggs laid per week by hens fed three kinds of feed. The student put "Average Eggs per Week" on the x-axis and "Type of Feed" on the y-axis. What is the problem?
column14: Nothing; the axes can go either way.
column15: The variables are switched: type of feed (independent) belongs on the x-axis and average eggs (dependent) on the y-axis.
column16: It should be a line graph.
column17: The y-axis needs a number scale from 0 to 100.
column28: The independent variable (type of feed) goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable (eggs) goes on the y-axis, so bars rise to show egg counts. A line graph would be wrong because feed types are separate categories.
column29: Which variable did the farmer choose, and which one was measured?

column9: Why should a graph of an experiment include the control group's results?
column14: The control gives a baseline to compare the experimental groups against.
column15: The control group is always the tallest bar.
column16: The control group shows the hypothesis is true.
column17: It shouldn't; the control group's data are thrown away.
column28: The control group shows what happens without the treatment, so readers can see how much the treatment changed the result. A common mistake is thinking control data get thrown away; without them, there is nothing to compare to.
column29: How would you know if the treatment made a difference if you didn't have anything to compare it to?

column9: Five students had their heart rates measured before and after 3 minutes of stair stepping. Which display would best let a reader compare each student's before and after heart rate?
column14: A pie chart of all the heart rates
column15: A bar graph with a "before" bar and an "after" bar for each student, plus a key
column16: A line graph of only the "after" heart rates
column17: A list of the students' favorite exercises
column28: Side-by-side bars for each student, with a key showing which is before and after, make the comparison easy. A pie chart is for parts of a whole, and showing only the "after" rates leaves nothing to compare.
column29: The reader needs to see two numbers next to each other for every student.

column9: Which statement is data (an observation) rather than an explanation?
column14: The mold grew because the bread was kept in a damp place.
column15: Mold probably likes warm kitchens.
column16: The bread got moldy because it was old.
column17: The mold covered 60% of the bread's surface after 5 days.
column28: "60% after 5 days" is a measurement, so it is data. The other choices try to explain why the mold grew (words like "because" and "probably" are clues). A common mistake is reporting explanations in the Results instead of the data.
column29: Which statement only reports what was measured, without a "because"?

column9: Data from 20 towns show that towns that sell more ice cream also have more cases of sunburn. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Eating ice cream causes sunburn.
column15: Sunburn makes people buy ice cream.
column16: The two are related, but the data do not show that one causes the other; hot, sunny weather could increase both.
column17: There is no relationship between ice cream sales and sunburn.
column28: The data show the two go up together, but that does not prove one causes the other. A third factor, sunny weather, could raise both. Jumping from "related" to "causes" is one of the most common mistakes in reading data.
column29: Is there something else that could make both numbers go up at the same time?

column9: A student's pie chart of a fox's diet shows rabbits 50%, mice 40%, and birds 30%. What is wrong?
column14: The percents add up to 120%, but the slices of a pie chart must add up to 100%.
column15: Nothing is wrong with the chart.
column16: Pie charts can't show animal diets.
column17: The slices should be listed from smallest to largest.
column28: 50 + 40 + 30 = 120%, but a pie chart shows one whole, so the slices must total 100%. There is a math or data error. A common mistake is checking each slice but never adding them up.
column29: Add the three percents together.

column9: A student measured her pulse after exercise in four trials: 120, 124, 122, and 60 beats per minute. The 60 happened because the pulse sensor slipped off her finger. What is the mean of the three valid trials, in beats per minute?
column28: Leave out the 60 because a known mistake caused it. 120 + 124 + 122 = 366, and 366 ÷ 3 = 122. A common mistake is including the 60, which gives 106.5.
column29: Which trial should not count? Average only the others.

column9: A student grew 4 radish plants: 2 with music playing and 2 without. The music plants grew 1 cm taller on average. The student concluded, "Music makes all plants grow faster." What is the best critique?
column14: The conclusion is fine because the music plants grew taller.
column15: The claim is too broad: only 4 radish plants were tested and the difference was small, so more trials and other kinds of plants are needed.
column16: The student should have played louder music.
column17: The conclusion should say music makes plants grow slower.
column28: Two plants per group is a tiny sample, a 1 cm difference could be chance, and only radishes were tested, so the claim about "all plants" goes far beyond the data. A common mistake is accepting any difference as proof.
column29: How many plants were tested, and what kind? Does the claim match that?

column9: Yeast cells in a flask (in thousands) were counted every 2 hours: 0 h: 10, 2 h: 40, 4 h: 160, 6 h: 400, 8 h: 480, 10 h: 490, 12 h: 490. Which sentence best describes the results?
column14: The population grew at the same rate the whole time.
column15: The population decreased after 6 hours.
column16: The population never changed.
column17: The population grew quickly at first, then leveled off at about 490 thousand cells.
column28: The count rose fast from 10 to 400 thousand, then barely changed (480, 490, 490), so the graph would rise and then level off. A common mistake is reading slower growth after 6 hours as a decrease; the numbers never went down.
column29: Compare how much the count changes in the early hours versus the late hours.

column9: A student counts the number of Daphnia in three tanks kept at different water temperatures every day for 10 days. Which graph communicates the results best?
column14: A pie chart for each day
column15: A line graph with time (days) on the x-axis, number of Daphnia on the y-axis, one line for each temperature, and a key
column16: A bar graph with number of Daphnia on the x-axis and temperatures on the y-axis
column17: A line graph with the temperatures on the x-axis and days on the y-axis
column28: The counts change over time, so a line graph with days on the x-axis and the count on the y-axis works best. Three tanks need three lines and a key to tell them apart. The other choices use the wrong graph or put variables on the wrong axes.
column29: What changes over time, and how will the reader tell the three tanks apart?

column9: Bean plants were grown in two soils. Group A heights: 12.4, 13.0, and 12.7 cm. Group B heights: 9.8, 10.4, and 10.1 cm. How much greater is Group A's average height than Group B's, in cm?
column28: Group A: 38.1 ÷ 3 = 12.7 cm. Group B: 30.3 ÷ 3 = 10.1 cm. 12.7 − 10.1 = 2.6 cm. A common mistake is subtracting the totals (38.1 − 30.3 = 7.8) instead of the averages.
column29: Find each group's average first, then subtract.

column9: Students tested how the number of hours of light per day (0, 4, 8, 12) affected the average number of algae cells per drop of pond water. Results: 5, 30, 60, and 85 cells per drop. Which one-sentence summary is the most complete AND concise?
column14: Algae grew.
column15: On the first day we set up four jars, then we put them under lamps, then we counted the cells under the microscope, and then we counted again later.
column16: Algae increased as light increased, from 5 cells per drop with 0 hours of light to 85 cells per drop with 12 hours of light per day.
column17: Algae decreased as light increased, from 85 to 5 cells per drop.
column28: The best summary names both variables, the direction of the trend, and the starting and ending numbers with units, in one sentence. "Algae grew" is too vague, the long sentence describes steps but no result, and the last choice gets the direction backward.
column29: A good summary tells what was changed, what happened, and gives numbers.

column9: A tadpole's length was 6 mm at week 1, 9 mm at week 2, 12 mm at week 3, and 15 mm at week 4. If this trend continues, what will its length be at week 7, in mm?
column28: It grows 3 mm each week. From week 4 to week 7 is 3 more weeks: 15 + 3 × 3 = 24 mm. A common mistake is adding only one more week (18 mm) or multiplying 7 × 3 = 21 without the starting length.
column29: Find how much it grows each week, then count the weeks from week 4 to week 7.

column9: A seedling's height was: day 0: 0 cm, day 2: 1 cm, day 4: 5 cm, day 6: 7 cm, day 8: 8 cm. Between which two days did it grow the fastest?
column14: Day 0 to day 2
column15: Day 2 to day 4
column16: Day 4 to day 6
column17: Day 6 to day 8
column28: Growth in each 2-day period: 1 cm, 4 cm, 2 cm, and 1 cm. The biggest jump (4 cm) was from day 2 to day 4, which is the steepest part of the graph. A common mistake is picking the period with the tallest heights (day 6 to 8) instead of the biggest change.
column29: Subtract to find how much it grew in each 2-day period.

column9: Mealworms were placed in the middle of a tray with oat bran on one side and cornmeal on the other. Averages over 5 trials of 10 mealworms: 5.2 ended on oat bran and 4.8 ended on cornmeal. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The mealworms showed no clear preference; the difference between the two sides was very small.
column15: Mealworms strongly prefer oat bran.
column16: Mealworms strongly prefer cornmeal.
column17: Mealworms cannot tell food apart, so they will starve.
column28: 5.2 versus 4.8 out of 10 is almost an even split, so the data don't show a clear preference. A common mistake is treating any difference, even a tiny one, as a strong result.
column29: If the mealworms didn't care at all, about how many would you expect on each side?

column9: A student's data table has three columns: "Plant," "Water," and "Height." The rows read: Plant 1, a little, 5; Plant 2, some, 8; Plant 3, a lot, 12. Select every problem with this table. Select all that apply.
column14: The water amounts are vague words instead of measured amounts like mL.
column15: The heights have no units.
column16: There is only one plant for each water amount, so there are no repeated trials.
column17: Numbers should never be written in a data table.
column18: The data should have been written in a paragraph instead.
column19: The table has too many columns.
column28: "A little" and "a lot" can't be repeated or compared exactly, the heights need units (cm?), and one plant per group means no repeated trials. Tables are exactly where numbers belong, and three columns is not too many.
column29: Could another scientist repeat this experiment and compare numbers using this table?

column9: Students tested whether a new plant food helps tomato plants grow. The plant-food group was kept by a sunny window, and the group without plant food was kept in a shady corner. The plant-food group grew taller. What should their conclusion say?
column14: The plant food makes tomato plants grow taller.
column15: Because the plant-food group also got more sunlight, the results can't show whether the plant food caused the difference; the test should be repeated with both groups in the same light.
column16: Sunlight has no effect on tomato plants.
column17: The graph should be changed so both groups look the same.
column28: Two things were different between the groups (plant food and sunlight), so there is no way to tell which one caused the extra growth. An honest conclusion says so and suggests a fair retest. A common mistake is giving the plant food credit anyway.
column29: Was the plant food the ONLY difference between the two groups?

column9: A deer herd decreased from 250 deer to 200 deer. By what percent did the herd decrease?
column28: The herd lost 250 − 200 = 50 deer. 50 ÷ 250 = 0.20, so it decreased by 20%. A common mistake is dividing by the new number (50 ÷ 200 = 25%) instead of the starting number.
column29: Find the change, then divide by the number you started with.

column9: Two lab groups each measured how far an earthworm crawled in 1 minute, using four trials. Group A: 10, 11, 10, 11 cm. Group B: 3, 18, 4, 17 cm. Both groups have a mean of 10.5 cm. Which statement best communicates the difference?
column14: The groups' results are exactly the same because their means match.
column15: Group B did better because it had the highest single trial.
column16: Group B's results are spread out much more, so its mean is less reliable than Group A's.
column17: Group A's data must be wrong because the trials are too close together.
column28: Same mean, but Group B's trials range from 3 to 18 cm while Group A's stay between 10 and 11 cm. Widely spread data make an average less reliable. A common mistake is looking only at the mean and ignoring how spread out the trials are.
column29: Compare the range of each group, not just the mean.

column9: An enzyme's activity (mL of oxygen per minute) was measured at five pH values: pH 2: 1, pH 4: 5, pH 6: 9, pH 8: 6, pH 10: 2. Which claim is supported by the data?
column14: The enzyme works best at exactly pH 7.
column15: Among the pH values tested, the enzyme worked fastest at pH 6.
column16: The enzyme stops working completely above pH 8.
column17: Enzyme activity increases as pH increases.
column28: The highest activity measured (9 mL/min) was at pH 6. pH 7 was never tested, so you can't claim it is best. The enzyme still worked at pH 10 (2 mL/min), and activity only rose up to pH 6 before falling.
column29: Only make claims about pH values that were actually tested.

column9: The largest value a student needs to graph is 240 seeds. The y-axis has 12 equal grid squares. What is the smallest whole number each square can stand for so that 240 still fits on the axis?
column28: 240 ÷ 12 = 20 seeds per square. A smaller value like 10 would only reach 120. A larger value like 25 fits but leaves the top of the graph empty.
column29: Divide the largest value by the number of squares.

column9: A student timed how long a pill bug took to roll into a ball in four planned trials. The first three took 6, 8, and 10 seconds. The fourth trial was never done, so the student wrote 0 seconds and reported the mean as 6 seconds. What is the problem?
column14: No problem; 6 seconds is the correct mean.
column15: The mean should be 10 seconds, the highest value.
column16: The student should report only the first trial, 6 seconds.
column17: The 0 is not real data; the mean of the three real trials is 8 seconds.
column28: Writing 0 for a trial that never happened adds fake data and drags the mean down: (6 + 8 + 10 + 0) ÷ 4 = 6. The real mean is (6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 3 = 8 seconds. A missing trial should be left blank or marked, not counted as 0.
column29: Did the pill bug really take 0 seconds in trial 4?

column9: Daphnia heart rates (beats per minute) were measured in four solutions, with 3 trials each. Put the solutions in order from LOWEST to HIGHEST average heart rate.
column14: Solution A: 200, 210, 220
column15: Solution B: 250, 230, 240
column16: Solution C: 190, 170, 180
column17: Solution D: 225, 215, 235
column28: Averages: C = 180, A = 210, D = 225, B = 240 beats per minute, so the order is C, A, D, B. Rank by each solution's average, not by one trial, because a single trial can be unusual.
column29: Find each solution's average first, then rank them.

column9: Students counted monarch butterflies at the same Wisconsin prairie each August: 2018: 300, 2019: 250, 2020: 180, 2021: 190, 2022: 130. Select every statement the data support. Select all that apply.
column14: Overall, the count decreased from 2018 to 2022.
column15: The count decreased every single year.
column16: The biggest one-year drop was from 2019 to 2020.
column17: The 2022 count was less than half of the 2018 count.
column18: Monarchs will be gone from this prairie by 2025.
column28: Overall the count fell from 300 to 130. Yearly changes: −50, −70, +10, −60, so the biggest drop was 2019 to 2020 and it did NOT fall every year (2021 rose). Half of 300 is 150, and 130 is less. The data can't tell us the future or the cause, so the last two are not supported.
column29: Work out the change from each year to the next before choosing.

column9: Match each weak statement from a lab report to its main problem.
column14: "Fertilizer is the best thing ever for plants." :: It is an opinion, not data.
column15: "The mice ate a lot more food." :: It is vague and gives no numbers.
column16: "We threw out trial 2 because it didn't match our hypothesis." :: It removes data only because they disagree with the prediction.
column17: A graph titled "Data" :: The title doesn't name the variables.
column28: Opinions aren't evidence; "a lot" needs numbers; data can't be tossed just for disagreeing with a hypothesis; and a title must name what was tested and measured. A common mix-up is calling the vague statement an opinion.
column29: For each one, ask: is it a feeling, missing numbers, dishonest, or unclear?

column9: On a line graph of the total number of oxygen bubbles counted from a water plant, the total was 8 bubbles at minute 2 and 28 bubbles at minute 6. What was the average rate between minute 2 and minute 6, in bubbles per minute?
column28: Change in bubbles: 28 − 8 = 20. Change in time: 6 − 2 = 4 minutes. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 bubbles per minute. A common mistake is dividing 28 by 6 or forgetting to subtract the starting values.
column29: Rate = change in bubbles ÷ change in time.

column9: A student's data table says the average mass of adult house mice was 22 kg. What is the most likely problem?
column14: The unit is wrong; adult house mice are about 22 grams, so the student probably meant g, not kg.
column15: The mice were fed too much.
column16: The number should be 2,200 kg.
column17: Nothing is wrong.
column28: 22 kg is about the mass of a medium-sized dog, so it can't be right for a mouse. Adult house mice are about 20 to 25 g, so the unit should be g. A wrong unit changes the meaning of the data by a factor of 1,000, which is why checking units matters.
column29: Does 22 kg make sense for an animal that fits in your hand?

column9: A student counted lichens on trees at different distances from a highway: 0 km: 2, 1 km: 8, 2 km: 15, 3 km: 21. The student wrote, "Lichens like being far from roads." Which is the best rewrite of this conclusion?
column14: Lichens hate highways.
column15: The number of lichens decreased as distance from the highway increased.
column16: The number of lichens increased as distance from the highway increased, from 2 at 0 km to 21 at 3 km.
column17: Lichens are found 21 km from the highway.
column28: The best rewrite describes the trend with the actual data and avoids guessing what lichens "like." The second choice reverses the trend, and the last confuses the count (21) with the distance (km).
column29: Replace the feeling word with what was actually counted.

column9: The mean of 5 reaction-time trials was 12 seconds. Four of the trials were 10, 13, 11, and 15 seconds. How many seconds was the fifth trial?
column28: Mean × number of trials = total: 12 × 5 = 60 seconds. The four known trials add to 49, so the fifth was 60 − 49 = 11 seconds. A common mistake is guessing the mean (12) for the missing value.
column29: If you know the mean and how many trials there were, you can find the total.
